opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends on what you believe your edge is, but there are a few things I'd say almost every serious robotics team has to own.

The first is the data engine. Robot learning isn't like vision or language, where you can scrape the internet and get most of the way there. The data that actually matters for your robot, your embodiment, your tasks, has to be collected, and *how* you collect it shapes everything downstream. That covers the teleoperation setup, the interfaces for human demonstrations, how you filter and curate, and how you decide what to collect next. If you outsource that, you've outsourced the thing that determines what your model can learn. In my lab we've spent a lot of time on this, on scalable ways to get human data and on how to make that data useful for robots, because I don't think it's a solved, plug-and-play layer yet.

The second is evaluation. Everyone wants to talk about models, but if you can't measure progress reliably, you're just fooling yourself. Real-world evaluation in robotics is noisy and expensive, and the details matter: initial conditions, object variation, what counts as success. A team needs to own its evaluation protocol, both in simulation and on real hardware, and be very disciplined about it. Otherwise you get a demo culture, where you show the best video out of fifty tries and nobody knows whether you've actually improved.

The third is the integration between learning and the physical system. I don't think every team has to build its own robot from scratch. Hardware is getting more commoditized, and that's a good thing. But you need people who deeply understand the loop: control frequencies, latency, sensing, calibration, how the policy's outputs actually turn into torques on the motors. A lot of failures that look like "the model isn't smart enough" are really systems issues. If nobody on the team can debug across that boundary, you'll be stuck.

What you can increasingly lean on others for are things like general pretrained vision and language backbones, simulation infrastructure, standard compute tooling, and, to some degree, off-the-shelf arms and grippers. Those are becoming shared foundations across the community.

So my short version is to own your data, own your evaluation, and own the glue between learning and the physical robot. Those are where the hard, unglamorous problems are, and they're also where the real differentiation comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says teams must collect robot-specific data in-house, but does not identify it as post-training data.

r002.rationale: It mentions filtering and curating task-specific robot data, not filtering pre-training data.

r003.rationale: It says data choices shape what a model can learn, but does not say each researcher must understand how particular data subsets affect system behavior.

r004.rationale: It warns against outsourcing data collection, but does not identify vendor-supplied data as opaque about how it was collected.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my honest take is that the thing you can never outsource is the data and the evaluation loop, because that's where your understanding of the problem actually lives.

Let me unpack that a bit. A lot of robotics today is becoming a learning problem, and in a learning problem the model architecture is increasingly a commodity. You can take an open-source policy architecture, a pretrained vision-language backbone, an off-the-shelf simulator, and you'll be roughly where everyone else is. That's fine. What differentiates a team is whether they know what the robot is actually bad at, and whether they have a tight loop between seeing a failure, collecting or synthesizing the right data to fix it, and verifying that the fix didn't break something else. That loop has to be in-house. If you hand your data collection to a vendor and your evaluation to a benchmark somebody else wrote, you lose the intuition about why things fail, and in robotics the why is almost everything.

The second thing I'd keep in-house is the interface between the learned system and the hardware. Not necessarily the hardware itself, lots of teams buy arms and grippers and that's completely reasonable, but the control stack, the safety layer, the latency budget, the way observations and actions are defined. Those decisions quietly shape what your policy can learn. I've seen teams where the policy looked wonderful in a notebook and then fell apart because the action space was mismatched with what the controller could track. Nobody outside the team is going to catch that for you.

And then the third, which is less technical, is the task specification. Deciding what success means, what the distribution of scenes and objects should be, what a human would consider acceptable behavior. That's a product question and a research question at the same time, and it has to come from the people who own the problem.

What I think you can and should outsource, or at least borrow, is almost everything else. Simulation engines, foundation models, teleoperation hardware, cloud infrastructure for training. The mistake I see is teams spending a year building their own simulator or their own motion planner out of pride, when the leverage was always in the data loop and the evaluation. Build the thing that teaches you about your problem. Buy the rest.

r002.rationale: It does not mention filtering pre-training data.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes understanding failures and evaluation, but does not say each researcher must understand how particular training-data subsets affect system behavior.

r004.rationale: It says outsourcing data collection loses intuition about why systems fail, but does not identify vendor-supplied data as opaque about how that data was collected.

astra-6.text:
I think the team needs to own the core learning loop: how you collect data, how you train the system, and how you evaluate whether it’s actually getting better at the task you care about. Those pieces are tightly connected. If something fails on the robot, you need to be able to trace that failure back and decide whether you need different data, a different model, or a change in the hardware.

That doesn’t mean you have to build every component yourself. You can use off-the-shelf hardware and existing software where they meet your needs. But the integration, and especially the understanding of what success looks like in your application, need to stay in-house. Otherwise, it’s very difficult to iterate effectively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the team needs to own the core loop of learning: understanding the task, collecting the right data, evaluating the robot, and using those failures to improve the system. Those pieces are tightly connected. If you outsource them entirely, you can lose the ability to understand why your robot works in one setting and fails in another.

That doesn’t mean you have to build every component yourself. You can use existing hardware, simulation tools, and pretrained models. But you need enough expertise in-house to integrate those components and judge whether they actually meet your requirements. The key is to own the parts that make your system useful for the particular problem you’re solving.
